[citation needed]

Full control of the team was turned over to Halas and Sternaman in 1921.  Official team and league records cite Halas as the founder as he took over the team in 1920 when it became a charter member of the NFL.

The team moved to Chicago in 1921, where the club was renamed the Chicago Staleys ; Under an agreement reached by Halas and Sternaman with Staley, they received US$5,000 to keep the name "Staleys" for the 1921 season.
In 1922, Halas changed the team name from the Staleys to the Bears .

The team moved into ___E:Wrigley Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field)___ , home of the ___E:Chicago Cubs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cubs)___ ___E:baseball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball)___ franchise.
As with several early NFL franchises, the Bears derived their nickname from their city's baseball team (bears' young are called "cubs").

Halas liked the bright orange-and-blue colors of his alma mater, the ___E:University of Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana%E2%80%93Champaign)___ , and the Bears adopted those colors as their own, albeit in a darker shade of each (the blue is ___E:Pantone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantone)___ 5395, ___E:navy blue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_blue)___ , and the orange is Pantone 1665, similar to burnt orange).
The Staleys/Bears dominated the league in the early years.

Their rivalry with the ___E:Chicago Cardinals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Cardinals)___ , the oldest in the NFL (and a crosstown rival from 1920 to 1959), was key in four out of the first six league titles.

During the league's first six years, the Bears lost twice to the ___E:Canton Bulldogs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Bulldogs)___ (who took two league titles over that span), and split with their crosstown rival Cardinals (going 4–4–2 against each other over that span), but no other team in the league defeated the Bears more than a single time. During that span, the Bears posted 34 shutouts. [citation needed]

The Bears' rivalry with the ___E:Green Bay Packers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers)___ is one of the oldest and most storied in American professional sports, dating back to 1921 (the Green Bay Packers were an independent team until they joined the NFL in 1921).

In one infamous incident that year, Halas got the Packers expelled from the league in order to prevent their signing a particular player, and then graciously got them re-admitted after the Bears had closed the deal with that player.
The franchise was an early success under Halas, capturing the NFL Championship in ___E:1921 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1921_NFL_season)___ and remaining competitive throughout the decade.

On December 7, 1924, the Bears claimed the Championship after defeating the ___E:Cleveland Bulldogs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Bulldogs)___ , even putting the title "World's Champions" on their 1924 team photo.
The NFL had ruled, however, that games after November 30 did not count towards league standings, and the Bears had to settle for second place behind Cleveland.
Their only losing season came in ___E:1929 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1929_NFL_season)___ . [citation needed]
During the 1920s the club was responsible for triggering the NFL's long-standing rule that a player could not be signed until his college's senior class had graduated.

The NFL took that action as a consequence of the Bears' aggressive signing of famous University of Illinois player ___E:Red Grange U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Grange)___ within a day of his final game as a collegian.
Despite much of the on-field success, the Bears were a team in trouble.
They faced the problem of increased operating costs and flatlined attendance.

The Bears would only draw roughly 5,000–6,000 fans a game, while a University of Chicago game would draw 40,000–50,000 fans a game. By adding top college football draw Red Grange to the roster, the Bears knew that they found something to draw more fans to their games. ___E:C.C. Pyle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C.C._Pyle)___ was able to secure a $2,000 per game contract for Grange, and in one of the first games, the Bears defeated the Green Bay Packers, 21–0. However, Grange remained on the sidelines while learning the team's plays from Bears quarterback ___E:Joey Sternaman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Sternaman)___ .

Later in 1925, the Bears went on a barnstorming tour, showing off the best football player of the day. 75,000 people paid to see Grange lead the Bears to a 17–7 victory over the Los Angeles Tigers, who were a quickly put together team of West Coast college all-stars.
After a loss to San Francisco, the Bears cruised to a 60–3 win over a semi-pro team called the Portland All Stars.
Any hopes that Grange would lead the Bears to glory in 1926 were quickly dashed.

A failed contract talk led to Grange bolting to a team in the newly-formed ___E:American Football League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League_(1926))___ (AFL), the ___E:New York Yankees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees_(NFL))___ , which was owned by Pyle. The Bears also lost star quarterback Joey Sternaman, who joined the ___E:Chicago Bulls of the AFL U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls_(AFL,_1926))___ .
The Bears replaced Grange with ___E:Paddy Driscoll U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Driscoll)___ , a star football player in his own right.
The Bears used the money made from the Grange barn-storming tour to sign the man who replaced him. Grange split his time between making movies and playing football.
However, the time was not right to have two competing pro football leagues, and the AFL folded after only one season.
Grange would return to the Bears.
After the financial losses of the ___E:1932 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_NFL_season)___ Championship season, Halas's partner Dutch Sternaman left the organization.
Halas maintained full control of the Bears until his death in 1983. He also coached the team off-and-on for forty seasons, an NFL record.

In the ___E:1932 "Unofficial" NFL Championship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Playoff_Game,_1932)___ , the Bears defeated the ___E:Portsmouth Spartans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Spartans)___ in the first NFL playoff game.  Due to blizzard conditions in Chicago, the game was played at ___E:Chicago Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Stadium)___ ,   marking it as the first indoor American football game. [citation needed]

[citation needed]

The team acquired the ___E:University of Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago)___ 's discarded nickname " ___E:Monsters of the Midway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsters_of_the_Midway)___ " and their famous helmet ___E:wishbone-C U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wishbone-C)___ , as well as a newly penned ___E:theme song U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_Down,_Chicago_Bears)___ that declared them "The Pride and Joy of Illinois".

Luckman established himself as one of the franchise's most elite quarterbacks.

After declining throughout the 1950s, the team rebounded in ___E:1963 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1963_NFL_season)___ to capture its eighth NFL Championship, which would be its last until 1985.  The late 1960s and early-1970s produced notable players like ___E:Dick Butkus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Butkus)___ , ___E:Gale Sayers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale_Sayers)___ , and ___E:Brian Piccolo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Piccolo)___ ,  who died of ___E:embryonal carcinoma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryonal_carcinoma)___ in 1970. Despite Hall of Fame careers, Butkus and Sayers would also have their careers cut short due to injuries, hamstringing the Bears of this era. [citation needed]
Halas retired as coach in ___E:1967 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Chicago_Bears_season)___ and spent the rest of his days in the front office.

As the only living founder of the NFL at the February 1970 ___E:merger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL-NFL_Merger)___ between the NFL and the ___E:American Football League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Football_League)___ , the owners honored Halas by electing him the first President of the ___E:National Football Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_Conference)___ , a position that he held until his death in 1983. He died from a rare form of liver cancer in 1999 at the age of 45.

On November 1, 1983, a day after the death of George Halas, his oldest daughter, Virginia McCaskey, took over as the majority owner of the team.  Her husband, ___E:Ed McCaskey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_McCaskey)___ , succeeded her father as the chairman of the board.

___E:Mike Ditka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ditka)___ , a ___E:tight end U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_end)___ for the Bears from ___E:1961 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961_Chicago_Bears_season)___ to ___E:1966 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Chicago_Bears_season)___ , was hired to coach the team by George Halas in ___E:1982 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Chicago_Bears_season)___ .

Throughout the remainder of his tenure, Ditka led the Bears to five more postseason berths, getting as far as the NFC Championship in the 1988 season.

In the 2001 season, Jim Miller took over as the primary starting quarterback and helped lead the Bears to a resurgent 13–3 record and division title.
The 2001 team did not see any postseason success as they fell 33–19 to the Philadelphia Eagles in the Divisional Round.
The 2002 season saw a setback as the team went 4–12.  The team improved to a 7–9 record in 2003 but still missed the postseason.
Jauron was fired after the 2003 season.

Soldier Field, located on ___E:Lake Shore Drive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Shore_Drive)___ in Chicago, is the home of the Bears.

After the ___E:AFL-NFL Merger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFL-NFL_Merger)___ , the league preferred their teams to play in stadiums that could hold at least 50,000 fans. Even with portable bleachers that the team set up at Wrigley, the stadium could still only hold 46,000.  At first, the Bears were supposed to play at Dyche Stadium (later called ___E:Ryan Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Field_(stadium))___ ), but ___E:Northwestern University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University)___ 's residential neighbors objected, and the agreement was cancelled.

The original home of the Bears was ___E:Staley Field U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staley_Field)___ at ___E:Decatur, Illinois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decatur,_Illinois)___ , when the team was known as the ___E:Decatur Staleys U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decatur_Staleys)___ , before they moved to Chicago in 1921. [citation needed]

Soldier Field's playing surface was changed from natural grass to ___E:astroturf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AstroTurf)___ before the 1971 season, and then back to natural grass in time for the start of the 1988 season.

Throughout its history, Soldier Field's field maintenance has been done by the ___E:Chicago Park District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Park_District)___ (the municipal entity from which the Bears lease the field) by disparate district employees, rather than a permanent team-employed grounds crew, generating some controversy among players for its rough surface.

This arrangement caused disagreements with the city throughout the years, with the Bears attempting to agree on a new stadium since 1986.  The stadium was the site of the infamous ___E:Fog Bowl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_Bowl_(American_football))___ playoff game between the Bears and ___E:Philadelphia Eagles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles)___ .
In ___E:2002 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Chicago_Bears_season)___ , the stadium was closed and rebuilt with only the exterior wall being preserved.
It was closed on Sunday, January 20, 2002, the day after the Bears lost in the ___E:playoffs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_NFL_playoffs)___ .
It reopened on September 27, 2003, after a complete rebuild (the second in the stadium's history).
Many fans refer to the rebuilt stadium as "New Soldier Field".

During the ___E:2002 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NFL_season)___ season, the Bears played their home games at the University of Illinois' ___E:Memorial Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Stadium_(University_of_Illinois))___ in ___E:Champaign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champaign,_Illinois)___ , where they went 3–5.
Multiple critics have negative views of the new stadium, believing that its structure has made it more of an eyesore than a landmark; some have dubbed it the "Mistake on the Lake".
Soldier Field was stripped of its ___E:National Historic Landmark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark)___ designation on February 17, 2006.

In the ___E:2005 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NFL_season)___ , the Bears won the NFC North Division and the No. 2 Seed in the NFC Playoffs, entitling them to play at least one home game in the postseason.
The team hosted (and lost) their divisional round match on January 15, 2006, against the ___E:Carolina Panthers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Carolina_Panthers_season)___ .
This was the first playoff game at Soldier Field since the stadium reopened.
The stadium's ___E:end zones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_zone)___ and midfield were unpainted until the ___E:1982 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_NFL_season)___ .
The design sported on the field included the bolded word "Chicago" rendered in ___E:Highway Gothic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_Gothic)___ in both end zones.
In 1983, the end zone design returned, with the addition of a large wishbone "C" Bears logo painted at midfield.
These field markings remained unchanged until the ___E:1996 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_NFL_season)___ .
In 1996 the midfield wishbone "C" was changed to a large blue Bears head, and the end zone design were painted with "Bears" in cursive.
This design remained until the ___E:1999 season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_NFL_season)___ , when the artwork was returned to the classic "Chicago" and "C".
In the new Soldier Field, the artwork was tweaked with the word "Chicago" bolded in one end zone and the other having "Bears".
